chunks: Common semiconductor materials. The question: What materials are typically used for semiconductors?
Semiconductors are made from several materials, and silicon is by far the most common. Each material has its own band gap and its own strengths.
Silicon wins on cost and ease of manufacture. Others, like gallium arsenide, are chosen when a special property is worth the cost: speed, light emission or high voltage.
Think of choosing a pan to cook with. A plain steel frying pan does almost every job well and is cheap, so most kitchens use it.
A copper saucepan heats faster, but costs more, so you use it only when speed matters. Silicon is the steel pan, and the others are the specialty pans.
The analogy only covers cost versus special ability, and not the actual physics.
On a log scale each material is a steep straight-ish line.

Germanium has the highest intrinsic density at room temperature and the highest leakage; silicon sits at 10^10; GaAs and especially SiC are many orders lower, which is why SiC devices can still behave as semiconductors at 500 degrees Celsius+ while silicon parts are normally rated only to about 150-175 degrees Celsius junction temperature (leakage climbs steeply above that, and lightly doped regions approach intrinsic behaviour near 200-250 degrees Celsius).
Band gap: the energy needed to free an electron, in eV (electron-volts, a tiny unit of energy). Mobility: how fast carriers move in a field.
Direct band gap: a gap where electrons can give off light easily, which suits LEDs and lasers. III-V compound: a mix of elements from groups III and V, such as gallium arsenide.
Wide-bandgap: materials with a large gap that handle high voltage and heat.
Compare gaps. Silicon has a band gap of about 1. 12 eV, which works well at room temperature. Germanium has about 0.
66 eV, which makes it leaky, so it is mostly used mixed with silicon (silicon-germanium) for fast radio-frequency (RF) circuits.
Gallium arsenide moves electrons faster and gives off light, so it suits RF and LEDs. That is the whole idea.
"Silicon is the workhorse because it's cheap, forms a great oxide, and has a good 1. 12 eV gap. Germanium is the older, leakier, 0. 66 eV material, now mostly used in SiGe.
III-V compounds like GaAs, InP and GaN are used for RF and optoelectronics because they have high electron mobility and direct bandgaps that emit light.
Silicon carbide and gallium nitride are wide-bandgap materials around 3. 3 eV used for high-voltage, high-temperature and fast power switching.
The choice is a trade between cost and a specific property."
